title: DNA Sequencing and DNA Profiling
subtitle: Reading DNA to diagnose genetic disease, and comparing profiles to trace inheritance
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate the use of technologies to determine inheritance patterns in a population using, for example: DNA sequencing and profiling (ACSBL064, ACSBL085)
Use examples to explain how biotechnologies diagnose genetic diseases
Discuss the roles of biological knowledge, genetic engineering and bioinformatics techniques used in biotechnology
inquiryQuestion: Can population genetic patterns be predicted with any accuracy?
lessonIntent: Students can explain how DNA sequencing and bioinformatics are used to diagnose genetic diseases such as cystic fibrosis, alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency and Leber congenital amaurosis, and distinguish sequencing from DNA profiling by what each produces.
examSkill: Match a diagnostic or inheritance question to the right technology, explain the steps from sample to diagnosis, and state what a result can and cannot show.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, DNA sequencing, diagnosing genetic disease, and DNA profiling. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: Twenty genes, one blind child
scenes.body: Leber congenital amaurosis can be caused by variants in more than twenty different genes. For one of them, RPE65, a gene therapy exists.
scenes.callout: How do you find which gene is faulty when there are twenty suspects?
scenes.caption: Sequencing identifies which of many genes causes a child's inherited blindness, which decides the treatment.

voiceover.text: Imagine a baby whose eyes don't seem to follow faces, and whose vision is fading. The diagnosis is Leber congenital amaurosis, an inherited blindness. But here's the problem. Variants in more than twenty different genes can cause it, and they all look much the same in the clinic. And it matters which gene it is, because for one of them, a gene called RPE65, there's now a gene therapy that can improve vision. So how do doctors find the one faulty gene among twenty suspects? They read the DNA itself. Today we'll see how DNA sequencing and bioinformatics diagnose genetic diseases, using cystic fibrosis, alpha one antitrypsin deficiency and inherited blindness as examples. Then we'll compare sequencing with DNA profiling, which answers a very different question.

scenes.heading: Sequencing reads the base order
scenes.body: DNA sequencing determines the exact order of the bases, A, T, C and G, in a stretch of DNA.

bullets.text: The output is the actual base order, so a specific variant can be seen directly.
Modern machines read millions of short fragments at the same time.
Computers assemble the overlapping reads back into the full sequence.

scenes.secondary: A chromosome is never read end to end in one pass. It is broken up, read in pieces, and put back together by software.
scenes.callout: Sequencing tells you the letters, in order.
scenes.caption: DNA sequencing reads the exact base order from millions of short fragments assembled by computer.

voiceover.text: So let's start with what sequencing actually does. DNA sequencing determines the exact order of the bases, the A's, T's, C's and G's, along a stretch of DNA. The output is literally the sequence of letters, which means that if a specific variant is present, like a single base substitution, you can see it directly. Modern sequencing machines don't read a chromosome from one end to the other, though. The DNA is broken into short fragments, millions of fragments are read at the same time, and then computer software lines up the overlapping reads and assembles them back into the full sequence. That's why sequencing and computing are now inseparable, and it leads us straight to bioinformatics.

scenes.heading: Bioinformatics turns reads into a diagnosis
scenes.body: Bioinformatics uses computing to compare a patient's sequence with a reference and with databases of known variants.

bullets.text: Align the patient's reads to a reference genome.
Flag positions where the patient differs: the variants.
Check each variant against databases of known harmful and harmless variants.

scenes.secondary: Most of the variants found are harmless. The skill is finding the one that fits the symptoms and the family history.
scenes.callout: The sequencer reads; the software interprets.
scenes.caption: Bioinformatics aligns reads, lists variants and checks them against databases to reach a diagnosis.

voiceover.text: Now, a pile of sequence reads isn't a diagnosis yet. That's where bioinformatics comes in, which is the use of computing to store, compare and analyse biological data. First, the patient's reads are aligned against a reference genome, a standard sequence everyone's DNA is compared with. Next, the software flags every position where the patient differs from the reference, and those differences are the variants. Then each variant is checked against databases that record which variants are known to cause disease, and which are harmless. Here's the thing, most of the variants any person carries are completely harmless. So the real skill is finding the one variant that fits the patient's symptoms and family history. The sequencer reads the DNA, but the software, and the scientists using it, interpret it.

scenes.heading: Diagnosing three genetic diseases
scenes.body: Each disease uses DNA technology a little differently, depending on how many genes and variants are involved.

bullets.text: Cystic fibrosis: newborn heel prick screen, DNA test for common CFTR variants, sweat test.
Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency: low protein in blood, then genotype the SERPINA1 gene.
Inherited retinal dystrophy and LCA: sequence a panel of many genes at once.

rows: Test for common variants, e.g. F508del
Genotype Z and S alleles, sequence if unclear

scenes.callout: One gene, few variants: targeted test. Many genes: sequence a panel.
scenes.caption: CF, alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency and LCA are diagnosed with targeted DNA tests or gene panel sequencing.

voiceover.text: Let's see this in three real diseases. Cystic fibrosis is caused by variants in the CFTR gene. In Australia, every newborn has a heel prick blood test. If a marker in the blood is high, the same sample is tested for the most common CFTR variants, such as F508del, a deletion of three bases, and a sweat test then confirms the diagnosis. Alpha one antitrypsin deficiency affects the lungs and liver. It's usually picked up by a low level of the protein in the blood, then the SERPINA1 gene is genotyped for the common Z and S alleles, and sequenced if the results don't add up. And for inherited retinal dystrophies, including LCA, so many genes are involved that labs sequence a whole panel of them at once. So the rule of thumb is simple. One gene with a few common variants, use a targeted test. Many possible genes, sequence a panel.

scenes.heading: Profiling compares patterns
scenes.body: DNA profiling compares the lengths of highly variable repeat regions, not the full base order.

bullets.text: It looks at short tandem repeats: short sequences repeated a variable number of times.
A person inherits one repeat length at each site from each parent.
Comparing profiles shows identity, relatedness and inheritance in families.

scenes.secondary: Profiling is used in forensics, paternity testing and conservation, but it cannot diagnose a disease, because the repeats it measures usually sit in noncoding DNA.
scenes.callout: Profiling matches patterns; it doesn't read every letter.
scenes.caption: DNA profiling compares STR repeat lengths to show identity and relatedness; it is not full sequencing.

voiceover.text: Now let's contrast that with DNA profiling, which works completely differently. Profiling doesn't read the base order at all. Instead, it measures a set of highly variable regions called short tandem repeats, where a short sequence is repeated over and over, and the number of repeats differs a lot between people. At each of those sites, you inherit one repeat length from your mother and one from your father. So by comparing profiles, you can tell whether two samples come from the same person, and whether people are related, which is how profiling traces inheritance in families and populations. It's used in forensics, paternity testing and even conservation breeding programs. But notice what it can't do. The repeats it measures usually sit in noncoding DNA, so a profile can't tell you whether someone has a genetic disease.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: DNA sequencing: determining the order of the bases in a stretch of DNA.
Bioinformatics: using computing to store, compare and analyse biological data.
Reference genome: a standard sequence that other genomes are compared against.
DNA profiling: comparing repeat lengths at selected sites to identify or relate samples.
Gene panel: a set of genes sequenced together for one group of conditions.

scenes.callout: Sequencing reads order; profiling compares repeat lengths.
scenes.caption: DNA sequencing, bioinformatics, reference genome, DNA profiling, gene panel.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the words. DNA sequencing is determining the order of the bases in a stretch of DNA. Bioinformatics is the use of computing to store, compare and analyse biological data, like sequences. A reference genome is a standard sequence that other genomes are compared against, and it's a composite, not any one real person. DNA profiling is comparing repeat lengths at a selected set of sites, to identify a sample or show relatedness. And a gene panel is a set of genes sequenced together because they're all linked to one group of conditions, like inherited blindness. Hold the contrast in one sentence. Sequencing reads the order of the bases, while profiling compares the lengths of repeats.

scenes.heading: Choose the technology
scenes.question: Choose DNA sequencing or DNA profiling for each, with a reason: (a) confirming which gene causes a child's inherited blindness; (b) testing whether a man is a child's biological father; (c) checking a baby with a high heel prick result for CFTR variants.
scenes.coachNote: Ask: do I need the actual bases in a gene, or just a pattern to compare between people?
steps: (a) Many genes could be responsible, so the bases must be read across a gene panel → sequencing.
(b) Paternity only needs a comparison of repeat lengths between child and man → profiling.
(c) The question is whether specific base changes are present in CFTR → a sequence based test.
Decision rule: need the bases in a gene, sequence; need to compare people, profile.
scenes.caption: (a) sequencing, (b) profiling, (c) sequencing: bases in a gene versus comparing people.

voiceover.text: Let's sort three scenarios, the way an exam might test you. The one question to ask each time is, do I need the actual bases in a gene, or just a pattern to compare between people? Part a, confirming which gene causes a child's inherited blindness. Many genes could be responsible, and you need to find the exact variant, so the bases have to be read across a gene panel. That's sequencing. Part b, testing whether a man is a child's biological father. You don't need any gene sequence at all, just a comparison of repeat lengths, where the child should share one at every site with the father. That's profiling. Part c, checking a baby with a high heel prick result for CFTR variants. The question is whether specific base changes are present in one gene, so that's a sequence based test again. So the rule is, if you need the bases in a gene, sequence it. If you need to compare people, profile them.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: treating a DNA profile as a full genome sequence. A profile measures repeat lengths at a few sites; it never reads the base order.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: thinking that finding a variant equals a diagnosis. Everyone carries thousands of variants. A variant only counts when databases, symptoms and family history show it causes the disease, and some remain of uncertain significance.
scenes.callout: A profile isn't a sequence, and a variant isn't a diagnosis.
scenes.caption: A profile is not a sequence; a variant becomes a diagnosis only when evidence links it to the disease.

voiceover.text: Two traps to avoid. Trap one, treating a DNA profile as if it were a full genome sequence. It isn't. A profile measures repeat lengths at a small set of sites, and it never reads the order of the bases. Different technology, different information. Trap two is more subtle, and it's straight from how diagnosis really works. Students assume that finding a variant is the same as making a diagnosis. But every one of us carries thousands of variants compared with the reference genome, and nearly all of them are harmless. A variant only counts as the cause when databases, the patient's symptoms and the family history all point the same way. And some variants simply can't be interpreted yet, so they're reported as variants of uncertain significance. So a profile isn't a sequence, and a variant isn't automatically a diagnosis.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A 40 year old non smoker has emphysema and a low level of alpha 1 antitrypsin in the blood. Outline how DNA technology would confirm the diagnosis, and why the family might also be tested.
answerSteps: The low protein level suggests alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency, but doesn't show the genetic cause.
Genotype the SERPINA1 gene for the common Z and S alleles; sequence the gene if the result doesn't match the protein level.
Two faulty alleles, such as ZZ, confirm the inherited deficiency.
It's inherited, so siblings may carry the same alleles and can be tested early and avoid smoking.
Answer: blood level, then SERPINA1 genotyping or sequencing, then family testing ✓
scenes.caption: Low alpha 1 antitrypsin, then SERPINA1 genotyping or sequencing confirms it; relatives can be tested too.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A forty year old who has never smoked develops emphysema, and a blood test shows a low level of alpha one antitrypsin. Outline how DNA technology would confirm the diagnosis, and explain why the family might be tested too. Pause and outline the steps. OK, here's the reasoning. The low protein level strongly suggests alpha one antitrypsin deficiency, but it doesn't show the genetic cause. So the next step is to genotype the SERPINA1 gene for the common faulty alleles, Z and S, and to sequence the whole gene if the result doesn't match the protein level. Finding two faulty alleles, like Z Z, confirms the inherited condition. And because it's inherited, brothers and sisters may carry the same alleles, so testing them means they can be monitored early, and warned never to smoke. Blood level, then genotyping or sequencing, then family testing.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: DNA sequencing reads the exact base order, from millions of short fragments assembled by computer.
Bioinformatics aligns reads to a reference, lists variants and checks them against databases.
CF and alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency use targeted variant tests; LCA uses gene panel sequencing.
DNA profiling compares repeat lengths to show identity and relatedness, not disease.
A variant is only a diagnosis when evidence links it to the disease.
scenes.finalPrompt: Need the bases in a gene? Sequence it. Need to compare people? Profile them. Then ask what the result can't show.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: sequencing, bioinformatics, three diagnoses, profiling, variant versus diagnosis.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five things to take away. First, DNA sequencing reads the exact order of the bases, from millions of short fragments that computers assemble. Second, bioinformatics turns those reads into information, aligning them to a reference, listing the variants and checking them against databases. Third, diagnosis depends on the disease. Cystic fibrosis and alpha one antitrypsin deficiency are usually confirmed with targeted tests for common variants, while inherited blindness like LCA needs a whole gene panel sequenced. Fourth, DNA profiling compares repeat lengths to show identity and relatedness, but it can't diagnose disease. And fifth, a variant only becomes a diagnosis when the evidence links it to the condition. So, if you need the bases in a gene, sequence it, and if you need to compare people, profile them.
